headline: 3 A.M. at The Race: One Cast, One Bass, and a Whole Different Bite
subhead: Warm water pushed the stripers nocturnal — the Race and Plum Gut are still delivering, but only if you're willing to fish in the dark.
body_markdown:
Third cast, 3:20 a.m., current screaming through The Race at what felt like every bit of five knots — a 9-inch black Gibbs pencil popper got hammered so hard I thought I'd hooked the bottom of the boat. Thirty-eight inches, girthy, came up out of the eddy behind Valiant Rock like she'd been sitting there waiting on the tide to turn. That fish told me everything I needed to know about this week: the daytime bite is dead, and the night bite is the whole program right now.

Water's warm across the board — New London's reading 69.4°F, and that's colder than the western Sound, which is pushing low-to-mid 70s. That gradient matters. Stripers don't like feeding hard in surface water that warm during daylight, so they've gone deep and nocturnal, exactly like I've seen every August when the thermocline sets up shallow and stable. The fish aren't gone. They're just smarter than the guys still soaking bunker chunks at noon.

The Race and Plum Gut are the two spots in this entire zone that stay productive through this pattern, and it's because the current keeps things churned and oxygenated even when the rest of the Sound goes flat and warm on top. I'm fishing the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, working the rip lines off Valiant Rock and the north side of Plum Gut with 2-ounce bucktails tipped with a chunk of pork rind, dropped into the seam and bounced along bottom in 25 to 40 feet. Eels still work if you can find them — a 10-inch live eel, slow-trolled or drifted through the same rip, has been my most consistent producer for the overslot class fish. Everything's coming on the dark side of the tide change, an hour before and after the current goes slack. Don't waste your time in the middle of a hard ebb — the fish are staged in the eddies, not fighting the main flow.

Bluefish are the other story right now, and they're not shy about daylight. Warm water is bluefish water, and Orient Point and the rip off Fishers Island have had jumbo blues mixed right in with slot bass on the same current edges, same boils, same structure. I've been running topwater — Super Strike poppers and 1-ounce metal — right into the surface commotion off the East End of Fishers, and it's producing double-digit blues in a morning along with the occasional bass that muscles its way into the feed. If you see birds working tight over a rip near Race Rock or the Fishers Island breakwater, don't overthink it — throw straight into the boil, not past it.

Fluke fishing has stayed exactly what we called it last week — steady, not spectacular. I've been drifting the sod banks and structure edges around Plum Gut and Orient Point Reef in 20 to 35 feet, and it's a mixed bag of shorts with enough keepers in the 18-to-22-inch range to make it worth the drift. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow along bottom on the last two hours of the incoming — that's been the combo. It's not a blitz bite. It's a grind-it-out bite, and that's fine by me in August.

Porgies and blackfish are still the reliable daytime program if you want something that doesn't require a 3 a.m. alarm. The reef structure off Fishers Island and the rock piles around Race Rock have been holding good numbers of porgies in 30 to 50 feet on sandworms and clam, and blackfish are starting to show on the deeper structure as the water stays stable — small green crabs on a jig head, worked tight to the rocks on slack tide, will get you into fish without much drama.

What's got me paying attention heading into next week is the moon. We're building toward the mid-August new moon, and that means tidal strength is ramping fast through The Race and Plum Gut. Historically this is exactly when the first false albacore and bonito show up on the edges of this corridor, pushed by the same current strength that's already stacking bait against the rocks at Fishers Island. I haven't seen albies yet this season in this zone, but the ingredients are lining up — squid pushing down from the Rhode Island side, stronger current, and warm stable water everywhere except right in the rips. If I had to bet, I'd say the first real showing happens within the next 7 to 10 days, and Fishers Island's east end will be the first place it happens.

If you've got one trip in you this week, fish it in the dark. Hit the last two hours of the ebb at Plum Gut with a bucktail or a live eel, work the eddies behind the rocks, and be patient — the bite window is short, maybe 45 minutes around the tide change, but it's real. Daytime, shift your focus to blues on the rip edges and fluke on the sod banks. That's the honest split right now: night for bass, day for everything else.
